o:
We split s into contiguous pieces so that no two pieces begin with the same letter, maximizing the piece count. Key observation: a piece can only start with a letter, and each letter can head at most one piece, so the count is capped by the number of distinct letters in s. Conversely, a greedy that cuts a new piece at the first occurrence of every not-yet-used letter achieves exactly that cap, because the first occurrence of any letter c cannot have been used as a start before (c hasn't appeared earlier at all).

Example 1: 'abab' has distinct letters {a,b} → 2. Example 2: 'abcd' → 4. Example 3: 'aaaa' → 1.
k: Upper bound = number of distinct characters
Greedy earliest-cut attains the bound: the first occurrence of each letter is always an eligible start

a.i: Scan left to right keeping a set of letters already used as piece starts. Whenever the current letter is unused, begin a new piece (increment count, mark the letter); otherwise extend the current piece. An exchange argument shows cutting as early as possible never reduces the final count.
s: For each character c: if c not in used, count++ and add c to used
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) set operations

a.n: Approach 2: Closed Form via Distinct Count
a.i: Since the greedy provably starts a piece at the first occurrence of every distinct letter, the answer equals the size of the alphabet set of s — computable in one line.
s: Insert all characters of s into a set
a.t: O(n) — single pass building a set

w: Lead with the observation that the answer is bounded by 26 and by the distinct-letter count; the greedy proof (first occurrences are always available) turns it into a one-liner. Pitfall: overcomplicating with DP — no choices matter beyond first occurrences. Follow-up: what if pieces had a minimum length, or starts had to be distinct AND adjacent pieces couldn't share any letter?
